item.title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
item.description:
Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s celsius this week, while regions in Indonesia grapple with wildfires

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.

Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”

item.title: Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
item.description:
Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise

The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.

Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.

item.title: Channel 4 film sheds new light on UK complicity in Gaza genocide
item.description:
Channel 4 film sheds new light on UK complicity in Gaza genocide

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 19:32
Investigation shows how the Foreign Office repeatedly failed to hold the Israeli army to account for war crimes
Pro-Palestinian activists and supporters gather in central London to protest British arms exports to Israel, on 17 April 2024 (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off

Twenty-five years have passed since sociologist Stanley Cohen asked a question that remains just as urgent today as it was when he first posed it.

How is it that institutions, governments and ordinary people can know about atrocities, mass killing and human rights abuses, but simultaneously manage to put them out of their minds?

His brilliant study, States of Denial: Knowing About Atrocities and Suffering, drew on Cohen’s own reporting of cover-ups, disappearances and torture in his native South Africa. Yet its examination of the ways in which we pretend to ourselves that terrible events are not taking place was broader, taking in Latin America, the Rwanda genocide, the Holocaust, the Middle East and other examples.

Cohen distinguished between the different ways in which politicians, journalists and others have suppressed knowledge of the truth. He identified what he called “literal denial” - the unblinking assertion that crimes are not taking place.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent speech to the United Nations contained numerous examples of literal denial. He said that the ratio of civilian casualties to combatants in Gaza was exceptionally low, that Israel did not block aid to Gaza, and that Hamas should be blamed for shortages.

He also made the nonsensical assertion that settler violence in the occupied West Bank was down to a “handful of young juvenile delinquents”. 

A Palestinian proverb, Yaktheb Al kithbah wa yusadikaha, roughly translates as: “He tells a lie, and then he believes it.” It describes the mental state of someone who has repeated the same falsehood so many times that eventually he or she has come to regard it as fact.

This may explain not just Netanyahu but also the army of apologists who blindly repeat what he says.

Cohen also paid attention to a more sophisticated form of denial which does challenge basic facts, but instead sanitises them in ways that seem reasonable or acceptable. He called this phenomenon “interpretative denial”.

Export licences 

Channel 4 recently published an hour-long documentary exploring how British ministers have employed the technique identified by Cohen as “interpretative denial”, to sanction Israel’s destruction of Gaza.

It is obvious to most people that Israel regularly commits crimes against humanity, with the newest Google Maps imagery showing total devastation across the enclave. Yet throughout this period, British ministers have denied Israeli war crimes. How have they managed this level of cognitive dissonance?

The Channel 4 film, Britain’s Gaza Secrets Exposed, went a long way to providing the answer. Over the past three years, British firms have exported millions of pounds worth of weaponry to Israel while it flattened Gaza and slaughtered civilians.

All those weapons need export licences. Under both domestic and international law, Britain is not allowed to export weapons to any country which it has reason to suspect commits war crimes.

This explains why, for the last three years, the Foreign Office unit that investigates potential breaches of humanitarian law has been busy assessing Israel’s military actions in Gaza.

Channel 4 reporter Ramita Navai obtained internal Foreign Office assessments of Israel’s conduct during the early stages of the war, dealing with hundreds of notorious cases. Her investigation shows that again and again, the British Foreign Office failed to hold the Israeli army to account.

It’s not just the government that is guilty of Cohen’s interpretative denial when it comes to the annihilation of Gaza. Most of the British media is equally complicit

Take the case of Hind Rajab, the five-year-old girl trapped in a car with her dead family after they were shot by Israeli soldiers. She spent three hours on the telephone asking for help. Eventually, permission came for rescuers, but when they did, soldiers shot dead both the rescuers and Hind herself. 

Unspeakable and hideous - but the Foreign Office assessors cited insufficient evidence to conclude that Israeli soldiers had breached international law.

Or take the air strike on al-Fakhoura school in Jabalia refugee camp in November 2023, which killed dozens of people, including women and children. The Foreign Office did not label this a war crime, even though the United Nations had clearly marked the school as a shelter for displaced civilians, and its coordinates had been given to the Israeli military. 

British officials managed to reach the same conclusion after 48 members of the Elian family were slaughtered in Nuseirat, and after Israel targeted a Medical Aid for Palestinians compound housing four British doctors. 

In only one case did the Foreign Office conclude that even a “possible” breach of international law had taken place. This was the Israeli strike that killed seven World Central Kitchen charity workers, including three British citizens. 

Despatches revealed that even as Israel pledged an “full, urgent and transparent” enquiry into the World Kitchen tragedy, then Foreign Secretary David Cameron was signing off yet another batch of approvals for arms exports - without waiting for the Israeli investigation to be completed.

Convenient findings

There’s little question that these repeated Foreign Office judgments were convenient. Throughout this period, Britain was an enthusiastic ally of Israel, and unwilling to offend the United States. 

So was the British legal process twisted in Israel’s favour? Channel 4 suggests it might have been. It secured an interview with Mark Smith, the only British official to have resigned over Gaza. 

His comments were devastating: “We’ve all seen the aerial footage of entire neighbourhoods literally flattened to the ground. They’ve destroyed the vast majority of all residential buildings in Gaza. I’ve never seen anything like it in my career, in my life.”

Smith went on: “So, even without being on the team and having access to the assessments being made, I could see, on the news, in broad daylight, with the naked eye, the most appalling attacks taking place on a daily basis. I mean, almost every single school, and almost every single hospital, in Gaza, has been damaged, or destroyed.

“How are we justifying our arms exports? If there is even a question whether domestically or internationally that a state that you are selling arms to might be conducting a genocide, then the time to be discussing whether they might be in breach of IHL is way gone.”

Smith says he stepped down after witnessing “illegality and complicity with war crimes” at the heart of government.

Why Palestine solidarity activists must keep up pressure on UK government 
Read More »

Channel 4 asked William Schabas, a leading human rights expert who comes from a family of Holocaust survivors, to comment on the Foreign Office’s judgement in the Hind Rajab tragedy. He replied: “When a child is killed in this manner, I think there has to be a very strong presumption that normally there cannot be any military justification or explanation for it.”

Channel 4 also spoke to Dearbhla Minogue, a lawyer with the Global Legal Action Network, which alongside the Palestinian NGO Al-Haq, took the UK government to court over its weapons exports to Israel. The groups lost, but the case led to the disclosure of the Foreign Office assessments analysed by Channel 4.

Minogue says that the British government used a rigged methodology which made identifying Israeli violations almost impossible. According to her, the Foreign Office legal team created a Catch 22 situation. In order to prove that a strike violated international humanitarian law, it required exact information on Israeli intentions.

Since Israel refused to provide this information the Foreign Office was unable to reach a conclusion on any incident, meaning that arms sales could continue.

This brings me to a final point.

The Channel 4 investigation has brought into the public domain a mass of fresh information that helps us to understand British complicity in the destruction of Gaza. 

Yet I have not found a single mainstream media outlet reporting its revelations. The explanation for this media omerta is simple: it’s not just the British government that is guilty of Cohen’s interpretative denial when it comes to the annihilation of Gaza. Most of the British media is equally complicit.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

item.title: Turkey supplies Korkut air defence systems to Ukraine, sources say
item.description:
Turkey supplies Korkut air defence systems to Ukraine, sources say

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 11:47
Ukrainian officials say anti-drone systems have proven effective against Russian attacks, with further purchases dependent on price
Chairman of Indonesian defence group Republikorps Norman Joesoef (L) shakes hands with Turkish defence company Aselsan's CEO Ahmet Akyol at an arms fair at the ExCeL centre, in London, on 9 September 2025 (Adrian Dennis/AFP)
Off

Turkey supplied anti-drone air defence systems to Ukraine earlier this year, allowing Kyiv to test new products and bolster its capabilities, several people familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye.

The sources said Ukraine had imported a small number of Turkish-made Korkut air defence systems, which typically consist of three weapon system vehicles and one command-and-control vehicle. They declined to disclose how many units had been deployed on the battlefield.

Produced by Aselsan, Korkut uses air defence guns to shoot down aerial targets, including the cruise missiles and drones that have become a persistent threat in the war in Ukraine. The system is designed to counter first-person-view and tethered drones using 25-millimetre smart ammunition.

“Korkut has been pretty much successful in countering the Russian attacks,” one Ukrainian official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity due to government restrictions. “There were of course some problems but nothing that couldn’t be overcome through some small adjustments.”

The official said Korkut could be considered battle-proven and that Ukraine was interested in purchasing more systems.

“If the pricing is right, we would like to buy more,” the official added.

Russia ties Black Sea grain deal with Ukraine to halt in oil refinery strikes
Read More »

Reports in 2021 suggested that Aselsan had offered to sell the systems to the Ukrainian army during a defence fair.

Ukrainian officials say many Turkish defence firms are now working with the Ukrainian army to test their weapons and improve their systems’ capabilities. Kyiv has welcomed these initiatives with open arms.

Aselsan CEO Ahmet Akyol told Turkish television over the weekend that Korkut systems were operational in nine countries. He said the Turkish army, Nato’s second-largest, was already using the systems and that Aselsan had begun exporting the technology after it had proven itself.

“We will announce new Korkut export contracts in coming days,” he said.

Middle East Eye reported in May that Saudi Arabia and Qatar had signed contracts to purchase Korkut 100/25 air defence systems. Iraq was also interested in acquiring the system.

Turkey has provided a wide variety of defensive weapons to Ukraine since the war started, first with Bayraktar TB2 drones and then laser-guided missiles, artillery rounds and machine guns.

item.title: Yemen’s child soldiers: How poverty and war are pushing minors to the frontlines
item.description:
Yemen’s child soldiers: How poverty and war are pushing minors to the frontlines

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 09:35
A 17-year-old fighter tells MEE he joined government-aligned forces to defend his village, as rights groups warn indoctrination is fuelling recruitment
A Yemeni boy carries a rifle during a Palestine solidarity rally in Sanaa, 12 July 2024 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

Ibrahim is 17, but he already knows how to handle a Kalashnikov.

He says he is not formally enlisted in the Yemeni government forces, but he fights shoulder to shoulder with his older brother and cousins.

“When the Houthis approached our village, many residents grabbed their personal weapons to resist them, and I was one of them.”

Ibrahim says that he took his father’s rifle and joined the fighting as part of the local resistance groups aligned with the Yemeni government forces.

“As a Yemeni, I know how to shoot because we have a Kalashnikov at home, which I've fired at weddings and other occasions,” Ibrahim told Middle East Eye.

He says he has no plans to pursue a military career and views the fighting as temporary, before resuming his studies to become an automotive engineer.

“We joined this battle to recapture our village from the Houthis. Once we achieve our goal, we will stop fighting,” he said.

Ibrahim is not the only child fighting alongside government-aligned forces.

As soon as the latest conflict flared in Yemen, child soldiers resurfaced alongside reciprocal accusations by warring parties over recruiting children and deploying them to the front lines. 

Neither side officially acknowledges recruiting minors; however, the United Nations, media outlets and human rights reports have confirmed that both parties engage in the practice.

A March 2025 report by the UN secretary-general on children and armed conflict documented 564 cases of child recruitment and use in Yemen between 2021 and 2023.

Of those, 345 were attributed to the Houthis and 210 to Yemen’s armed forces and affiliated armed groups. The remaining cases were attributed to unidentified perpetrators and the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant in Yemen.

The UN said the children ranged from 8 to 17 years old. It verified 293 children being recruited and used in combat, while 187 were used in support roles as guards at military checkpoints, informants and drivers.

Twenty-seven of those used in combat were under 15.

Official denial    

Ahmed, Ibrahim’s 41-year-old cousin, said that Ibrahim does not participate in active combat on the front lines. Instead, he performs support tasks positioned behind the troops, arguing that his physical build enables him to handle the duties.

“Fighting on the front lines requires experience - it’s not easy for just anyone to fight there,” Ahmed told MEE. 

‘We must enter first’: Yemen’s female soldiers face war, danger and a changing society
Read More »

“Fighters like Ibrahim can provide crucial support behind the main forces and play an important role in such difficult circumstances.”

As fighting between Houthi and government-aligned forces intensified around Taiz last month, a BBC team aired an interview with a 16-year-old fighter associated with government forces who said he had participated in active combat. 

Responding to the report, Colonel Abdul Basit al-Bahr, deputy head of the Moral Guidance Department at the Taiz Axis Command, told MEE that the boy was accompanying his father and was not acting as a combatant for government forces.

“We in the armed forces have a clear stance on child recruitment; it is strictly prohibited, and children cannot be accepted into the ranks of the armed forces or thrust into military operations.”

Yet he acknowledged that government forces encounter children on the battlefield, with some as young as 10 years old. 

“Appropriate legal and humanitarian measures are taken regarding them, and they are referred to the relevant authorities to handle their situation in accordance with the law,” Bahr said, adding that minors captured while fighting alongside the Houthis are treated as children rather than adult combatants.

Poverty drives recruitment   

The SAM Organisation for Rights and Liberties has documented the recruitment of 11,310 children from 2014 to February 2023.

According to the independent advocacy group monitoring violations in Yemen, the figures include 6,269 children aged eight to 11. 

Yemenis seek safety in Djibouti as African migrants continue arriving in Yemen
Read More »

Tawfeeq al-Homaidi, president of SAM, said the economic collapse caused by years of war has created conditions in which armed groups can exploit children and their families. 

“When a family loses its income, the breadwinner stops receiving a salary, and a child is pushed out of school, the small sum of money, food ration, or stipend offered by an armed group becomes a matter of basic survival rather than a choice,” Homaidi told MEE.

In a joint statement issued on 26 September 2026, the Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom, alongside 266 Yemeni human rights and civil society organisations, condemned the exploitation of children by the Houthis, highlighting how severe economic distress is weaponised to force minors onto the battlefield.

“Children bore the brunt of these violations through forced recruitment, being thrust into battlefields, and the exploitation of their needs and their families' socioeconomic hardships through ideological and military indoctrination,” the statement read.

“However, reducing recruitment strictly to poverty is a mistake,” Homaidi cautioned.

“There is a broader spectrum of causes, such as ideological mobilisation, the exploitation of schools and summer camps, social and tribal pressure, the lure of status, weapons, and money, interrupted schooling, and in some cases, direct coercion.”

Ideology and promises  

Minors were lured to the front lines with promises of a personal Kalashnikov rifle, a one-month military training course, and a monthly stipend of 50,000 Yemeni riyals (approximately $94), a report published last month by Al Jazeera English from Houthi-controlled areas revealed. 

Homaidi added that recent UN statements on Yemen have highlighted severe concerns over child recruitment, specifically citing Houthi-run summer camps where thousands of children are subjected to military training and sectarian content. 

Saudi war against Houthis displaces 130,000 Yemenis as hunger crisis deepens
Read More »

The Houthis have faced particular scrutiny over their recruitment and indoctrination of children, but the phenomenon is not limited to Houthi forces.

“Child recruitment is not confined solely to Houthi-controlled areas,” Homaidi stressed.

“According to the UN, cases have been documented among government forces and affiliated or allied armed formations as well, albeit in far smaller numbers and generally without coercion.”

According to UN Ocha estimates for 2026, over 22 million people in Yemen remain in urgent need of humanitarian assistance and protection services, including 5.2 million internally displaced persons. 

The renewed fighting, however, is creating new opportunities for armed groups to draw children into the conflict, whether through formal recruitment, local armed formations, family pressure or economic desperation.

The UN's definition of recruitment is broader than formal enlistment, encompassing children used in combat as well as in support roles.

For Ibrahim, however, the distinction between a formal soldier and a young man carrying a rifle alongside government forces is meaningless.

He says he is fighting to reclaim his village.

The names of child soldiers have been changed on request.

item.title: Can Baghdad gain control over paramilitary groups amid US war on Iran?
item.description:
Can Baghdad gain control over paramilitary groups amid US war on Iran?

Submitted by Zahra Ladha on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 10:18
As the state seeks to bring armed groups under its control, competing interests and external pressures stand in the way
Popular Mobilisation Forces stand guard during a symbolic funeral procession celebrating the withdrawal of the US-led coalition from Iraq, in Baghdad on 1 October 2026 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
Off

With the US withdrawing its forces from its territories, Iraq is moving towards bringing the country’s powerful paramilitary groups under greater state control, a process that will require navigating competing interests among the groups, Baghdad and Washington.

It is unlikely to amount to straightforward disarmament, instead seeking to limit these groups’ ability to act autonomously by bringing their weapons more closely under state control and, in some cases, integrating fighters into formal state structures. Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has now set a deadline of 30 June 2027 to complete this process. 

Whether the process succeeds will depend on Baghdad’s ability to manage the demands of armed groups, their willingness to accept limits on their autonomy and, crucially, whether external actors avoid actions that could undermine it.

In recent weeks, a framework for enforcing state control over Iraq’s paramilitary groups has emerged.

According to Zaidi, Baghdad plans to implement the process in phases, starting with a 90-day cessation of military activity. This period began on 30 September, on the same day the US-led coalition, which has for years come under attacks by these groups, officially withdrew from Iraq. 

In return, the US would refrain from launching military strikes on armed groups in Iraq.

During the United States' war on Iran, the US military repeatedly struck bases affiliated with Iran-linked paramilitaries, including the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF). On 29 July, Saudi Arabia and the US launched a joint attack on PMF targets, killing at least 20 members.

Following the three-month period, paramilitary groups, many of which formerly operated under the PMF and are already embedded within the state, will begin the process of bringing their weapons under state control.

What this means in practice remains unclear. According to a statement made on 2 September by Nouri al-Maliki, leader of the State of Law Coalition and a former Iraqi prime minister, the process is not disarmament in the traditional sense, but the containment and control of weapons by the state.

Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
Read More »

Maliki also indicated that this process may not include all types of arms, and that the focus is likely to be on weapons that can be used to launch attacks on "foreign and local targets".

Iran-linked armed groups in Iraq have over the years launched rocket attacks, one-way attack drone and long-range missile attacks on US interests in Iraq and the wider region, and reportedly against energy and other strategic infrastructure in the Gulf.

The process also aims to limit these groups’ ability to undertake unilateral military action beyond Iraq’s borders, reducing the risk of Iraq being drawn into regional escalation.

Actions by these groups, including drone strikes on Israel during the war in Gaza and attacks on US interests during the war on Iran, have previously risked doing just that.

Baghdad also appears to be seeking to integrate fighters from some paramiltaries operating outside the PMF into its ranks as individuals, rather than preserving their existing command structures. Without naming the groups involved, Zaidi said in an interview in late September that his goal was “to end the existence of these factions as independent entities”.

For many of these groups, however, accepting a proposal that limits their ability to launch military attacks and operate autonomously would require guarantees that Baghdad would be willing to protect their interests.

Meeting demands 

Iraq’s array of paramilitary groups, with varying degrees of proximity to Iran, wield different levels of political and economic influence. These dynamics are likely to shape the bargaining process between the groups and Baghdad.

Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq (AAH) and Kataeb Imam Ali, announced in June that they would place their arms under state control. For AAH, however, continued willingness to do so is likely contingent on its ability to preserve its economic influence and the parliamentary seats held by its affiliated Sadiqoon bloc.

At the time, more hardline factions such as Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba and Kataeb Hezbollah – which, under the banner of the Islamic Resistance of Iraq (IRI), participated in recent attacks on US interests in the region – refused to disarm. These groups have cited the continued US presence in Iraq, among other factors, as a reason for retaining their weapons.

However, in late August, these groups announced conditions for placing their weapons under state control. On the day of the US-led coalition’s withdrawal from Iraq, Kataeb Hezbollah said it would halt all military activity except against hostile aircraft.

The move broadly aligns with Zaidi’s efforts to de-escalate tensions before bringing these groups under tighter state control.

There has been progress on some of the key demands put forward by these groups.

On 1 October, Ankara announced that the Bashiqa-Zelikan military camp near Mosul would be handed to the Iraqi government under an agreed mechanism and timetable, meeting a key demand of paramilitary groups for the withdrawal of Turkish troops from northern Iraq.

In parallel, efforts are underway to remove the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) from the area, another demand made by the groups.

Still, Baghdad may find it difficult to meet all of their demands. In August, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq called for the “liberation” of Iraq’s political and economic decision-making from US “hegemony”. Paramilitary groups affiliated with the IRI have previously cited US control over Iraq’s oil revenues as an example.

Since 2003, Iraq’s oil revenues have been held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and transferred to Iraq monthly in US dollars.

Notably, groups including Kataeb Hezbollah, Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada, Harakat al-Nujaba and Ansar Allah al-Awfiya have in recent months called for strengthening Iraq’s air defences and preventing foreign aircraft from using Iraqi airspace to strike neighbouring countries, including Iran. 

Any renewed US strikes on Iran, particularly during the 90-day period, could therefore undermine efforts to integrate some Iraqi armed groups and increase the risk of clashes between these groups and Baghdad.

A balancing act

Iraq’s prime minister can bring paramilitary weapons under state control only if he can balance the interests of these groups with those of Washington.

The extent of state control, how far the state will go in dismantling autonomous command structures, and where these groups will fit within Iraq’s state structures remain subject to debate. The implementation of the plan will therefore depend on whether all key parties are willing to avoid maximalist positions that could stall the process.

“Washington has not expressed an opposing stance to Zaidi’s current proposal, or to the militia’s demands. But clarity around Washington’s red lines are required for the process to move forward,” Mustafa al-Saray, director of research at the Bayan Centre for Strategic Studies, an Iraq-based think tank, told Middle East Eye.

With US troops departing, Iraq looks beyond balancing Washington and Tehran
Read More »

“Similarly, even though most of these militias appear receptive to Zaidi’s plan, there is always a chance that Tehran objects to the process, and this would also change the negotiation process in Iraq.”

Iran-linked groups in Iraq have already demonstrated their readiness to challenge decisions made by Baghdad.

On 25 September, Iraq suspended all flights to Iran after the US announced sweeping secondary sanctions on the Iranian aviation industry. But after a Kataeb Hezbollah security official warned that Zaidi’s government could be “brought down”, Washington granted a one-month sanctions waiver allowing Iraqi Airways to operate flights between Iran and the Shia holy city of Najaf.

Still, if Zaidi fails to manage competing interests in Baghdad and Washington, Iraqi paramilitary groups could turn against the new prime minister, who came to power in May after the US effectively vetoed their preferred candidate.

“There is a real risk that Iraq returns to the pre-2022 equation, where the militias held prime ministers directly responsible for international actions against them,” said Saray.

Renewed and sustained US strikes on Iran would also likely undermine prospects for a peaceful integration process.

As seen during the previous escalation, Baghdad would likely struggle to prevent some Iraqi armed groups from launching attacks in support of Iran, potentially derailing the current de-escalation.

Moreover, like after the US-Saudi strikes on the PMF in late July, further foreign attacks on Iraq’s paramilitaries would almost certainly harden their stance against accepting greater state oversight.

item.title: Making a Killing: Who profits from slaughter in Gaza and Yemen?
item.description:
Making a Killing: Who profits from slaughter in Gaza and Yemen?

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 17:23
New book by Andrew Feinstein traces $50bn in profit from the genocide in Gaza
BAE Systems' stand at the Defence and Security Equipment International fair at the ExCeL centre, in east London, on 9 September 2025 (AFP/Adrian Dennis)
Off

“The global trade in weapons is a business that counts its profits in billions, and its losses in human lives.” 

This devastating balance sheet is the subject of Making a Killing: How the West Profits from Slaughter in Gaza and Yemen, a new book by arms corruption investigative organisation Shadow World Investigations, co-authored by Andrew Feinstein, Ruth Rohde and Jack Cinamon. 

In it, they trace the rivers of blood that flow from the ruins of Gaza and Yemen into backroom meetings with politicians and arms manufacturing CEOs, exposing the corruption at the heart of the military-industrial complex – less a virus infecting the industry, but rather its lifeblood, keeping it alive.

The project began in 2017 with the intention of chronicling the Yemen crisis, but the authors incorporated Gaza after the start of the genocide in October 2023. 

Due to be published in November, the work conveys the urgency and immediacy of conflicts coming to define the collapse of international order and the moral supremacy once claimed by western democracies. 

Suffice to say, while the losses are never felt by the profiteers of war, the book delivers its own eulogy to some of its victims, through the voices of Palestinian journalist Ahmed Alnaouq, and the founders of Yemen-based Mwatana for Human Rights, Radhya al-Mutawakel and Abdulrasheed al-Faqih. 

Mwatana is an organisation which aims to document civilian casualties from the war in Yemen not being recorded in international or regional media.

Alnaouq, author of We Are Not Numbers, had three generations of his family wiped out in a single Israeli air strike on his home in Gaza.

In the book, he harrowingly recounts how he found out in a message from a friend in Gaza reading: “Airstrike. Everyone killed.”

“Israel thought that killing my family would silence me, that it would break me,” he says, “but they could not have anticipated that this would give my life a new purpose.

“More than ever, my life now has meaning, a clear and determined goal: to find out who murdered my family, who profited from the murder of my family.” 

The quest to answer this question becomes the driving force of the investigation that Feinstein, Rohde and Cinamon embark on.

Illegal and legal corruption

Although a lesser known conflict, the authors recount in great detail the history of the war in Yemen and how it has been enabled by Western arms – a reality still ongoing after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently pledged to continue supporting Saudi Arabia amid the latest escalation with Yemen’s Houthis.

The relationship between western powers and Saudi Arabia – explained simply by then Crown Prince Fahd as trading oil for security – has long been rife with bribery and illegality.

Miliband ‘looking at’ whether Palestine Action ban was sensible, argues mass arrests 'unintended'
Read More »

The Al-Yamamah arms deal between Saudi Arabia and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher was the largest in UK history, with up to £6bn ($7.94bn) allegedly paid in bribes and lavish gifts to Saudi royals, intermediaries, and others – including Thatcher’s own son – by the firm known today as BAE Systems, the UK’s largest weapons company.

Despite making up just half a percent of global trade, arms deals account for an estimated 40 percent of corruption cases.

Such corruption is facilitated by opaque deals, made with taxpayer money, hidden behind high security clearances lest our enemies get hold of such valuable information.

While some corruption is overt, much of it is systematic, they explain, with manufacturers like BAE Systems routinely treated as an arm of the state. 

What is often referred to as a “revolving door” between government officials and arms lobbyists could more accurately be described as an “open plan office” – or, as Tony Blair’s foreign secretary once remarked of BAE Systems, having the key to 10 Downing Street’s garden door. 

US hegemony 

It is not the products themselves, whose value is usually over-inflated bordering on a rip-off, but the company’s ability to influence government that enables this relationship to take place, the authors argue.

In this way, the blood-soaked cash circulates back through the grubby hands of corrupt politicians, lobby groups and think tanks and into the lifeblood of our democracy, thwarting foreign policy to facilitate further accumulation of private profit at any cost. 

It is not a bug, but rather the system working as intended.

“The arms trade is the backbone of state power under US hegemony,” the authors argue: with Israel and Saudi Arabia representing two “strategic poles” of maintaining US power in the Middle East. 

“I never for a moment understood ‘never again’ as being just about us Jews” Andrew Feinstein speaks about how his mum hid from the Gestapo during the Holocaust Full episode: https://t.co/39N8aGAm59 https://t.co/TJRcLiPEq3

— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) June 11, 2024

Yemen and Gaza signify the global shift from European colonial power to the post-war period of “US-centred political and economic order”.

Within this, elites of all nationalities collaborate with each other and arms bosses for their own personal enrichment and to sustain a system that allows them to continue getting fat on profits.

This is why foreign policy often seems to take place outside the realm of democratic contestation, with decisions made in some out-of-view corporate suite unaffected by the millions of people that take to the streets in protest.

“The corrupt arms trade is dragging us inexorably into a world in which even liberal democracies are becoming the best democracies money can buy,” they write.

Forever wars

Quoting George Orwell’s 1984, the authors write that “the consciousness of being at war, and therefore in danger, makes the handing-over of all power to a small caste seem the natural, unavoidable condition of survival”.

Thus defence spending is sold as being in the public interest, keeping us safe – even as it soaks up money that could be going into public services.

There are always magic money trees for war.

Meddling in foreign affairs by funnelling weaponry into unstable regional conflicts carries certain risks, including what is known as blowback.

From arming the mujahideen in Afghanistan to fight to the Soviets to supporting Saddam Hussein in the Iran-Iraq war, the US has a habit of having their friends turn into enemies overnight

“Blowback,” the book explains, “illustrates how the cavalier global distribution of weapons can fuel the very instability that the arms trade and defence establishment claim to guard against.” 

From arming the mujihadeen in Afghanistan against the Soviets to supporting Saddam Hussein in the Iran-Iraq war, the US has a habit of having their friends turn into enemies overnight. 

But when pockets are lined by instability and violence, blowback is experienced as a benefit, while risk is outsourced to ordinary people in the region: another villain created for the war on terror to target, another opportunity to rile up the public into supporting endless wars under the guise of “defence”.

In some instances, this is explicit. 

Israel Ziv, former head of the Israeli army’s Operations Directorate and founder of Global CST, a security services firm which orchestrated Israeli weapons exports, was sanctioned by the US government for supplying weapons to both sides of the conflict in South Sudan, while simultaneously profiting from contracts to solve the humanitarian crisis he helped create. 

Similarly, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who led the UK into an illegal invasion of Iraq and lied to the public about its weapons of mass destruction, has capitalised on his failures since leaving office, most notably sitting on Trump’s “Board of Peace” to reconstruct Gaza. 

“While Palestinians sift through 60 million tonnes of rubble, Blair and his allies are already planning how to monetise the rebuild,” Feinstein, Rohde and Cinamon write. 

Andrew Feinstein: The anti-apartheid activist trying to stop Keir Starmer
Read More »

“The man who helped break the region is now selling himself as the one to fix it – for a fee.” 

Making a Killing lays bare how executives and politicians arranged a price for human lives in corporate boardrooms, never having to face the cost of their actions halfway across the world. 

The book’s investigation calculated the final sum of the profit accumulated from levelling Gaza, destroying countless families like Alnaouq’s, to be $50bn. 

The rich and powerful involved in the “Board of Peace” hope to generate further profits by transforming Gaza into a real estate free-for-all, as an AI video posted by Trump suggested.

Israeli technology is marketed as “battle-tested” in Gaza and exported to conflicts around the world, as well as being used for domestic surveillance to counter anti-government protest.

Bloodbaths like Gaza and Yemen are treated as “laboratories” for high-tech weaponry then sold at extortionate prices at arms fairs.

The answer to the question “who made the bomb that killed my family” exposes the greed and corruption inherent to an industry whose model of growth relies on death and destruction, which lies at the centre of western hegemony. 

Making a Killing: How the West Profits from Slaughter in Gaza and Yemen by Andrew Feinstein, Ruth Rohde and Jack Cinamon is published by Verso

item.title: Yemen's Saudi-backed forces claim key gains around Bab al-Mandab strait
item.description:
Yemen's Saudi-backed forces claim key gains around Bab al-Mandab strait

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said on Monday that they had seized key positions on the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Houthis.

Three military sources and one government source told Reuters their forces had taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks the strategically vital strait, and that they were asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition.

The forces are fighting to reverse significant advances made by the Iran-aligned Houthis and to drive them from the Bab al-Mandab.

Houthi-aligned media had earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area.

item.title: Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?
item.description:
Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?

Submitted by Yunus Turhan on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 16:33
When past leaders have tried to govern from a single centre, the country's peripheries have united in opposition
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed attends a meeting in Moscow on 25 September 2025 (Evgenia Novozhenina/AFP)
On

Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it. 

Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. 

Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut. This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout.

Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement, a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself.

For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it.

After the Zemane Mesafint (“Era of the Princes”) in the 18th and 19th centuries, when regional lords ran their own affairs, Tewodros II tried to rebuild the empire by the sword. The provinces revolted one after another, and in 1868, he died at Magdala, his army reduced to remnants.

Similarly, former emperor Haile Selassie’s 1962 dissolution of the Eritrean federation turned a small insurgency into a 30-year war. The Derg regime pushed centralisation to its limits, and fell in 1991 to a coalition of ethno-regional groups, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF). 

The 1995 constitution swung back by creating ethnic federalism and, in Article 39, even a right to secession. Yet the EPRDF ran that system through party discipline from Addis Ababa, so self-rule stayed largely on paper. 

In short, Ethiopia’s state structure has swung between centralisation and decentralisation over 170 years.

Tensions unresolved

Abiy assumed power in 2018 by preaching Medemer, an approach of reconciliation and national unity in the face of ethnic divisions. But it quickly began to unravel in 2019, when he dissolved the EPRDF to form his Prosperity Party. 

Tensions long kept under wraps soon boiled over, and to contain them, Abiy returned to the tools of his predecessors: mass arrests of suspected opponents, and new restrictions on the media.

War with the TPLF followed in 2020, fought alongside forces from Eritrea and Amhara. After the Pretoria agreement in 2022, Abiy disbanded the regional special forces, which pushed the Fano militia into open revolt. The status of Welkait and Raya, claimed by both Amhara and Tigray, was left unresolved after Pretoria, so both sides felt cheated.

The coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war

What made such an unlikely alliance possible? The answer lies less with the rebels than with the centre’s own choices. Each centralising step cost Abiy a partner. 

Eritrea, kept away from the Pretoria negotiating table, watched its old enemy survive, and then heard Addis Ababa speak of a Red Sea port in terms Asmara read as a claim on Assab. The special forces decision did the same to Amhara. 

In short, the coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war. 

Can the new alliance muster the capacity to challenge Abiy’s rule? This is not likely, at least for the time being. The alliance has named no joint military commander, and unlike 1991, it has no dominant force able to march on the capital. 

Abiy has a drone fleet the Derg never had, along with a fresh mandate from the public, as his party won 438 of the 501 contested seats in parliament (nearly 90 percent) this past June. But some groups have rejected the results, and voting did not take place in Tigray, which comprises 38 constituencies.

The road ahead

Three paths seem possible from here for Abiy. In the first, he peels Amhara away with concessions over Welkait, while the TPLF’s seizure of airports enables him to present it as the aggressor. The price is that any Welkait deal with Fano locks Tigray into permanent war, so dividing the alliance on one front deepens the other. 

In the second, the war settles into a stalemate: the centre holds the cities and the skies, armed movements hold the countryside, and Ethiopia drifts towards a de facto confederation run by men with guns - a Zemene Mesafint by other means. 

The third is the most dangerous. Abiy has a record of seeking a unifying cause abroad when pressed at home; once it was the Renaissance Dam (where Egypt is a factor), and today it is access to the sea. This time, a move towards Assab would turn a civil war into a war with Eritrea, and pull in every regional power watching.

The regional map explains why that third path cannot be dismissed. The fault lines of Sudan’s war now run through Ethiopia. On one side sits the UAE, Abiy’s main supporter since 2018, whose drones are widely credited with turning the last war, and which analysts accuse of routing arms through Ethiopia to Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces.

Gold, arms and mercenaries: On UAE's shadowy networks in Sudan
Read More »

Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, widely seen as brokered by Abu Dhabi, and President Isaac Herzog’s visit to Addis Ababa in February tied Ethiopia’s hunger for the sea to Emirati-Israeli designs for the Red Sea. 

On the other side, Egypt, which regards the Renaissance Dam as a threat to its survival, has built an axis with Eritrea and Somalia, and backs Sudan’s army, with Saudi Arabia reportedly drawing closer to Asmara. 

A simultaneous rift with Egypt and Eritrea would carry a heavy price for Abiy Ahmed's government, since Addis Ababa would then face hostile fault lines to both its north and its east.

Cairo has pledged troops to the African Union mission in Somalia, and Eritrea has already placed itself at the heart of the dispute by severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia altogether.

Hemmed in on both flanks, Ethiopia would depend almost entirely on Djibouti, which already handles close to 90 percent of its trade.

For Ahmed, a war on several fronts would revive what Otto von Bismarck called his "cauchemar des coalitions", the "nightmare of coalitions" in which France and Russia might join forces and drag Germany into a two-front war.

Fighting at home while quarrelling abroad would be the worst of all scenarios for Addis Ababa, once the military costs, the strain on debt relief and the human toll are counted together.

For Cairo, an Ethiopia tied down at home is leverage on the Nile. For Abu Dhabi, a collapsing Ethiopia would mean losing its most valuable partner on the mainland. Both camps thus have reasons to feed the war, yet neither has much interest in a clear winner. That is how civil wars become proxy wars. 

This is where Turkey matters. It brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia in December 2024, while holding its largest overseas base in Mogadishu, and has mended ties with both Cairo and Abu Dhabi in recent years. This gives Ankara a rare ability to speak to both camps. As his room at home narrows, Abiy may well knock on Ankara’s door again.

Ethiopia’s prognosis therefore hinges on Abiy’s next move: whether he adopts collaborative, win-win strategies towards his opponents, or clings to a zero-sum game. In making that choice, he would do well to look back, for Ethiopian history is clear on one point: the state has held when power was bargained with the regions, and it has cracked whenever power was imposed on them. 

The reason is simple. Once power has been devolved to the peripheries, it can rarely be recentralised without resistance - and this is precisely the lesson Abiy must now come to terms with.
